primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: A previously alloimmunized patient can have a red-cell alloantibody titer that falls below pretransfusion detection. Re-exposure to the corresponding minor red-cell antigen triggers a rapid secondary (anamnestic) antibody response, causing delayed destruction of transfused erythrocytes.
vignette: A 51-year-old man who received packed red blood cells after trauma 7 years ago is admitted for gastrointestinal bleeding and receives crossmatch-compatible packed red blood cells. His pretransfusion antibody screen is negative. One week later, he has fatigue and mild jaundice. His hemoglobin has fallen toward the pretransfusion value, indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase are increased, and haptoglobin is decreased. The direct antiglobulin test is positive, and repeat antibody testing now detects anti-Jkᵃ.
lead: Which mechanism best explains this transfusion reaction?
correct: A secondary alloantibody response to a previously encountered minor red-cell antigen whose antibody level had become undetectable
distractors: Preexisting IgM antibodies against ABO antigens causing rapid complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis
Donor anti-HLA antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary microvasculature
Recipient anti-IgA antibodies reacting with donor plasma proteins and causing systemic anaphylaxis
Viable donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking recipient tissues
distractor_notes: ABO-incompatible acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are driven by preexisting antibodies and occur during or soon after transfusion, not after a symptom-free interval of about a week with a newly detectable minor-antigen alloantibody.

Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies are associated with transfusion-related acute lung injury, which presents with acute hypoxemia and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than delayed DAT-positive hemolysis.
Anti-IgA-mediated reactions cause immediate allergic/anaphylactic manifestations in susceptible IgA-deficient recipients, not a delayed fall in hemoglobin with newly detectable anti-Jkᵃ.

Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease is caused by engrafted donor lymphocytes and produces a different syndrome, classically including fever, rash, gastrointestinal disease, liver injury, and marrow failure rather than isolated delayed alloimmune red-cell destruction.
key_expl: This is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Remote transfusion can prime memory B cells against a minor red-cell antigen. Over time, the circulating alloantibody concentration may fall below the detection threshold of routine pretransfusion testing, so the current antibody screen and crossmatch can appear compatible. Re-exposure to antigen-positive donor erythrocytes then triggers an anamnestic antibody response, with delayed hemolysis and a newly positive direct antiglobulin test. Kidd-system antibodies are a classic cause because they can become difficult to detect between exposures and then rise rapidly after re-exposure.
objective: Recognize delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction as an anamnestic alloantibody response to a previously encountered minor red-cell antigen after the circulating antibody has fallen below pretransfusion detection.
